summary: The docs already hold a strong spine (a white pawn wins by becoming free, not royal; a child who must learn to let go; five bosses that are five beliefs) but almost none of it can reach the player yet. As built, story is one HUD label, six hardcoded room one-liners and one child line, with no story flags, dialogue, cutscene, title, ending or localization layer. The research converges on six things for a small 2D game with little text: (1) let mechanics carry the theme, so the pawn's unlock of a move is the story beat and the final unassisted diagonal step is the payload; (2) spend dialogue sparingly in short bark-style lines with a per-speaker blip rather than voice; (3) put the lore in diegetic objects (the Book of House Rules, props, the child's blue crayon); (4) make death and retry part of the relationship (the existing 'THE CHILD RESETS THE BOARD' line); (5) treat control as the game's currency and take it from the player only for beats that matter (the Black King's lock); (6) design the peak and the ending first, because memory weights them. The deepest emotional engine is already latent in gdd.md:355-361: the war began as a child's lonely game and the Queen warns that a world without rules gets abandoned. Child-development sources say children use toys as their words and replay frightening events while changing the outcome, so a lost war replayed by a child is a truthful frame. The owner has to decide what that loss is (it never needs to be said aloud). Recommended structure is a hybrid: macro three-act for pacing (it needs a low point and a climax), micro kishotenketsu per district (the existing room formula in full-gameplay-design-v2.md:627-638), and a dusk-to-morning 'one night' frame as the thread. The base should ship a complete placeholder script for every beat, each tagged with its purpose and emotion so the owner can rewrite words and art without losing intent. It should be built on built-in Godot features first (Resource sequences, RichTextLabel typewriter, AnimationPlayer method tracks, TranslationServer) because CLAUDE.md requires built-ins before addons; Dialogue Manager 4 (MIT, Godot 4.6+) is the only addon that fits a GDScript-only project, and only if the owner agrees to a dependency. Items flagged 'proposal' in the other fields (the rules-as-ruler motif, the night frame, writing the pawn's own rule) are my suggestions, not decisions in the docs.
premise_analysis:
WHAT THE STORY ALREADY IS (and is strong)
- Spine: a white pawn survives a rigged war, is noticed by a child, crosses the bedroom and defeats the Black King 'without becoming part of the old rule system'; it wins by being free, not by promoting (docs/design/nar1-story-outline-spec.md:11-17). Only NAR.1 has owner approval (2026-09-30, nar1:3); NAR.2-6 are agent drafts (audit: /tmp/audit/result.json, lane ui_narrative).
- Emotional ladder: defeat, loneliness, agency, recognition, trust, pressure, independence, partnership, freedom (nar1:21-33), mapped onto Acts 0-6 plus a morning ending (nar1:39-48).
- Bosses are beliefs, not just HP bars: pride in status, faith in written rules, force and walls, control and performance, a rule system pretending to be a person (nar1:93-99). Their resolutions are already story-as-mechanic: the child blocks a lane and the pawn wins on timing (docs/design/gdd.md:393), the pawn crosses a crayon line the Bishop says is not real (gdd.md:400), the Rook breaks its own throne (gdd.md:407), child and pawn cooperate without controlling each other (gdd.md:414), the pawn takes a diagonal step by choice (gdd.md:421; docs/design/enemy-behavior-bible.md:382-390). This is ludonarrative harmony by design; Hocking's 'dissonance' is the failure case where mechanics contradict the story (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludonarrative_dissonance).
- The child is a companion who 'learns to let the pawn act alone' (gdd.md:441), help changes the room not enemy HP (docs/design/full-gameplay-design-v2.md:674), blue means child-made (gdd.md:484), the child appears as a hand, shadow, drawings and voice (gdd.md:462).
- Tone: serious grief, no gore, humor from scale and material (gdd.md:447-449). The Hollow Knight narrative review's lesson that cute characters can carry a dark story supports this (https://media.gdcvault.com/gdc2020/GameNarrativeReview/Gabriel%20St.%20Onge_Hollow%20Knight%20Narrative%20Review.pdf).
- Best existing writing: the Book of House Rules flavor lines, e.g. 'The child wrote it in the margin, and the board obeyed.' (resources/rules/backstep_pawn.tres:11) and 'Nobody told it the first move was over.' (resources/rules/charging_pawn.tres:11). They put the child in the world without a single cutscene. The default defeat subtitle 'THE CHILD RESETS THE BOARD' (scripts/main.gd:296; docs/soulslike-world-plan.md:94) already makes retry diegetic.
- Hidden gold in the GDD: the midpoint reveal that the battle began as a story the child was playing alone (gdd.md:355) and the Queen telling the child that a world without rules will be abandoned and forgotten (gdd.md:360-361). That is the real emotional engine: fear that play ends and toys get put away. Child-development sources say toys are a child's words, that children express fear and guilt through toys and may replay a frightening event while changing its outcome (https://files.eric.ed.gov/fulltext/ED430172.pdf). Winnicott describes the toy as occupying a space between imagination and outer reality that a child should never be forced to resolve (https://www.encyclopedia.com/psychology/dictionaries-thesauruses-pictures-and-press-releases/transitional-object). Design rule that follows: never explain whether the pawn is 'really' alive. The bedroom shows the toy truth, the board shows the felt truth, and the blue crayon crosses both.

WHAT IS MISSING OR CONTRADICTORY
1. Delivery infrastructure is close to zero. Story reaches the player through one HUD label (scripts/ui/hud.gd:83-85), six hardcoded room one-liners (scenes/rooms/t1_white_kings_fall.tscn:11, t2_fallen_sword_tile.tscn:12, t3_first_pawn_clash.tscn:11, t4_broken_rule_yard.tscn:16, b1_black_pawn_captain.tscn:16, h1_chess_rug_hub.tscn:10) and one child line (t2_fallen_sword_tile.tscn:56). WorldState stores no story flags (scripts/world/world_state.gd:10-22). There is no dialogue, cutscene, title, pause, credits, ending or localization (docs/where-we-are.md:97; audit UI.2-UI.6, NAR.2-NAR.6). The strings sit in scripts, against the CLAUDE.md data-not-code rule (audit UI.2).
2. Contradictions to settle. (a) When the child first speaks: the T2 whisper 'take it' (t2_fallen_sword_tile.tscn:56) and the GDD prologue whisper 'Try another way' (gdd.md:323) contradict the T1 spec and flow map, which say no child voice until after B1 (docs/production/t1-white-kings-fall-production-spec.md:278-280; docs/production/act-1-opening-to-first-boss-flow-map.md:563-567). (b) Three endings: the pawn refuses promotion and the child rebuilds the playground (gdd.md:375-380); the child places the pawn back as its own kind of piece (v2:546-558); the pawn stands outside the board by a blue line and the child leaves it there (nar1:105-118, docs/design/nar6-ending-script-spec.md:11-19, the approved one). (c) Region names and boss titles differ between gdd.md:276-299/386-423 and v2/nar1. (d) The GDD says no collectible lore documents (gdd.md:435) while the soulslike plan makes the Book of House Rules the lore channel (docs/soulslike-world-plan.md:107-113). (e) The pawn 'believes the child is a god' (gdd.md:272) versus a child who is 'not all-knowing' (nar1:77).
3. The child has a function but not a feeling. The docs list what the child does (block, path, rotate, nudge: gdd.md:237-268) but not what the child feels or what loss the war replays. The pawn has no personality beats. The black side must not be purely evil (nar1:139) yet has no pathos. Allies and rescues are one line (gdd.md:434, 547).
4. Boss story is a rule list (docs/design/nar5-boss-dialogue-behavior-beats-spec.md:11-17) plus one data-only captain with a single message (b1_black_pawn_captain.tscn:16); no boss has phases, so no phase or defeat beat can fire (audit EN lane, NAR.5).
5. Legibility: HUD text is 7-9 px on 640x360 and no text reveal exists (audit UI.6). Xbox guidance of 28 px at 1080p is about 9 px at 360p, and Vietnamese diacritics need roughly 10 px and extra line height (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/gaming/accessibility/xbox-accessibility-guidelines/104). Vietnamese pixel-font coverage must be tested, not assumed.

EMOTION RESEARCH THAT SHOULD SHAPE THE BASE
- Two rewards: enjoyment tracks gameplay plus competence and autonomy; appreciation (meaningfulness, poignancy) tracks story plus insight and relatedness (Oliver et al., https://digitalcommons.butler.edu/ccom_papers/145/). A tight-combat base serves only one. Relatedness is a separate need in self-determination theory (https://selfdeterminationtheory.org/SDT/documents/2006_RyanRigbyPrzybylski_MandE.pdf), and the child is this game's relatedness engine.
- Lazzaro: players move between four kinds of fun and strong games offer at least three; Hard Fun yields fiero, Easy Fun curiosity, Serious Fun meaning (https://www.nicolelazzaro.com/the4-keys-to-fun/). Combat is Hard Fun, bedroom exploration is Easy Fun, the pawn-child bond is Serious Fun.
- Peak-end: memory weights the peak and the ending (https://dl.acm.org/doi/fullHtml/10.1145/3582437.3587195), so the Queen reveal, the King's box-closing and the last five minutes must be designed first and funded most.
- Ueda built Ico around one relationship and said the studio put all its money on Yorda (https://puzzlebyrinth.com/en/articles/designer-ueda). Spend the narrative budget on the child.

OWNER DECISIONS THE BASE CANNOT MAKE (it should hold placeholders)
(a) What loss is the child replaying (never has to be spoken)? (b) Source language for text (the owner writes to me in Vietnamese) and whether Vietnamese or English ships first. (c) The moment the child first speaks. (d) Which ending. (e) Proposal: a unifying motif already latent in the assets, where 'rule' means chess rule, house rule and ruler. The Black Captain wields a ruler blade (resources/enemies/black_pawn_captain.tres:9) and the toolset is pencil and eraser; the black side could be the child's own 'rules' (bedtime, homework, tidy-up) made into pieces, with morning as the release. This is my reading, not in the docs.

delivery_techniques.technique: Environmental / indexical storytelling (props as traces of the past)
delivery_techniques.how_it_works: Props, layout and light imply what happened before the player arrived; Carson's rule set: cause-and-effect props (scorch marks, a fallen piano) hint at past events and pull players forward, the world's rules must not be broken or players feel cheated, and orient the player ('Where am I?') by clues not exposition (https://www.gamedeveloper.com/design/environmental-storytelling-creating-immersive-3d-worlds-using-lessons-learned-from-the-theme-park-industry). Jenkins calls this 'embedded narrative', clues and artifacts the player assembles, and argues designers act as narrative architects (http://web.mit.edu/~21fms/People/henry3/games&narrative.html). Fernandez-Vara's 'indexical' version is strongest when reading the traces is needed to play (https://dspace.mit.edu/handle/1721.1/100274). Smith and Worch's GDC 2010 definition: stage player-space so props can be read as a meaningful whole (https://alexx-kay.livejournal.com/284287.html).
delivery_techniques.example_game: Unpacking: no characters, dialogue or cutscenes; a life story from 1,000 objects, with gaps between moves left for players to infer (https://www.gamedeveloper.com/marketing/unpacking-a-narrative-through-1-000-household-items). Hollow Knight: the aftermath of a fallen capital is shown, not told (GDC review PDF above). Hyper Light Drifter: ruins and bodies hint at history (https://www.killscreen.com/building-wordless-world-hyper-light-drifter/).
delivery_techniques.cost_to_build: Low code, high content labour. Base needs: an Inspectable prop marker (press confirm: one line or an icon bubble), a StateVariant node that shows/hides/swaps props by story flag (e.g. rug scattered vs tidied, hub evolution gdd.md:303-310), and a per-room 'what happened here' field in the room data. Art placement is the owner's work.
delivery_techniques.fit_for_us: Highest. A child's bedroom is the ideal indexical space (tape, crayon, half-finished drawing, a lamp left on) and blue already means 'child-made' (gdd.md:484). T1 is built on this idea (docs/production/t1-white-kings-fall-production-spec.md:61-72). Make 'what happened here' a required line in every room spec, and Unpacking's lesson applies: every object sends a message whether intended or not, so place each one on purpose.

delivery_techniques.how_it_works: The verb the player performs is the statement. Celeste hands Madeline an extra dash only after she accepts Badeline, so growth is a new move (https://epiloguegaming.com/playing-the-narrative-celeste/). Gris begins unable to jump and each new ability arrives with the story (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gris). Brothers puts each brother on one stick and trigger, and the ending asks the player to use the missing brother's side (https://kotaku.com/brothers-tale-of-two-sons-remake-ending-older-younger-1851302128; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brothers:_A_Tale_of_Two_Sons). Papers, Please makes dense paperwork under time pressure feel like bureaucracy (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludonarrative_dissonance; https://www.firstpersonscholar.com/the-art-of-papers-please/). Undertale gives Mercy a full action system while Fight is deliberately thin (https://dl.acm.org/doi/full/10.1145/3815598.3815657).
delivery_techniques.example_game: Celeste, Gris, Brothers: A Tale of Two Sons, Papers, Please, Undertale
delivery_techniques.cost_to_build: Mostly design, little code. Needs a DirectionLock component and restore events (the King's Lock Direction already exists on paper: enemy-behavior-bible.md:361), a 'control budget' (see the sequencer), and events that mark each unlock as a story beat.
delivery_techniques.fit_for_us: The premise is already a mechanic metaphor (chess rules to freedom). The task is to protect it: no XP/promotion upgrades (leveling was cut: soulslike-world-plan.md:96-97), each boss unlock should negate that boss's belief, and the final diagonal step must be a move the player has been denied all game.

delivery_techniques.technique: Diegetic text: the Book of House Rules, weapon and item descriptions
delivery_techniques.how_it_works: Lore lives in an object the player opens by choice. Miyazaki says he deliberately held information back so players become one with the story and much of it sits in item descriptions (fan-translated podcast: http://soulslore.wikidot.com/das1-game-no-shokutaku). Tunic's manual is recovered page by page, written in an unreadable script, physically worn, and teaches through pictures (https://blog.playstation.com/2022/09/21/the-creation-of-tunics-invaluable-in-game-manual/). Hollow Knight scatters lore in tablets and biased NPC accounts, with the downside that vital lore is easy to miss (GDC review PDF above).
delivery_techniques.example_game: Dark Souls item descriptions, Tunic's manual, Hollow Knight lore tablets
delivery_techniques.cost_to_build: Low; the RuleEntry/RuleBook resources and B-key UI already exist (scripts/data/rule_entry.gd, scripts/ui/rule_book_ui.gd). Add: a margin_note field (the child's handwriting), a crossed-out/rewritten page state, pages for bosses and weapons, unlock on 'seen in combat' not zone load, and a world pause while open (audit UI.3 gaps).
delivery_techniques.fit_for_us: High and already the best-written channel. Keep it optional (docs/design/ui3-rule-book-design-spec.md:21-30). Make it the one place the child's handwriting appears so reading it feels like reading the child. Each Souls-style weapon description (Wooden Sword, Pencil) can be one line of toy-world poetry.

delivery_techniques.how_it_works: A bark is a short line fired by a game event, not a conversation. Craft rules: carry personality and implied situation, not only information; layer context; write many variants (https://www.thenarrativedept.com/blog/barks; https://www.gamedeveloper.com/game-platforms/8-key-principles-of-writing-effective-game-dialogue). Redding's Far Cry 2 GDC 2009 talk covered the states a bark must convey (https://kotaku.com/why-video-game-characters-say-such-ridiculous-things-5921878). Barks must not replace visual storytelling (same Kotaku article).
delivery_techniques.example_game: Far Cry 2, Hades (every death and victory triggers new dialogue: https://gdconf.com/news/dive-dialogue-hades-gdc-2021)
delivery_techniques.cost_to_build: Medium. BarkTable resource: trigger event type, speaker, candidate lines with weight, priority, cooldown, once-only, conditions on flags/counters, and a selector in the presentation bridge that plays at most one bark at a time. Content is the bulk.
delivery_techniques.fit_for_us: High, but bounded by NAR.3 (short, emotional before instructional, never a tutorial robot: docs/design/nar3-child-voice-rules-spec.md:11-18) and by 'dialogue never obscures active danger cells' (gdd.md:522). Ration child barks so each lands; the pawn 'barks' as an emote icon, never words; white survivors and black pieces get barks keyed to the rule they hold.

delivery_techniques.technique: Short in-engine dialogue with a per-speaker blip instead of voice
delivery_techniques.how_it_works: Two to four lines, texting-style fragments, advanced by the player. A Short Hike's writer wrote dialogue in short snippets like text messages and kept NPC chat brief for pacing (https://gamepilgrim.com/2020/02/26/developer-interview-adam-robinson-yu/). Undertale and Animal Crossing give each character a distinct blip or pitch per letter instead of voice acting (https://geolojosh.itch.io/goodlands/devlog/314373/how-to-animal-crossing-dialogue-sounds). Godot's RichTextLabel supports typewriter reveal via visible_ratio and BBCode effects such as wave and shake for emotion (https://docs.godotengine.org/en/stable/classes/class_richtextlabel.html; https://docs.godotengine.org/en/stable/tutorials/ui/bbcode_in_richtextlabel.html).
delivery_techniques.example_game: A Short Hike, Undertale, Animal Crossing
delivery_techniques.cost_to_build: Low-medium. A DialogueSequence resource, a Speaker resource (name key, color, blip stream, portrait or icon set), and one presenter scene using built-in nodes. No addon is needed unless branching is wanted.
delivery_techniques.fit_for_us: High: gdd.md:431 asks for conversations 'usually under four lines', gdd.md:557 puts voice acting out of scope, and blips make translation cheap (no re-recording). Distinguish voices by sound and color: child = close, soft, blue-tinged; kingdom voices = 'subtle imagined resonance' (gdd.md:508).

delivery_techniques.technique: Wordless panel sequences (the child's drawings as comic panels)
delivery_techniques.how_it_works: Dialogue is shown as a handful of images instead of words. Hyper Light Drifter's team decided at the start to have no text at all; conversations are image panels, and sequences run to about five images (https://www.killscreen.com/building-wordless-world-hyper-light-drifter/). The creator compares the approach to Pixar's wordless openings (https://www.gamedeveloper.com/business/the-ultra-modern-stylings-of-hyper-light-drifter).
delivery_techniques.cost_to_build: Low code (a PanelSequence presenter: image, hold time, transition, optional sound), art-heavy and fully the owner's. Zero translation cost.
delivery_techniques.fit_for_us: High and especially suited to this owner: crayon panels are literally the child's imagination made visible and sidestep the AI-art-quality concern. Good for the prologue, the Queen's address to the child, and the ending/credits. Keep the NAR.2 rule that the opening be understandable without exposition (docs/design/nar2-opening-script-spec.md:23-30).

delivery_techniques.technique: In-engine beat sequencer that preserves or deliberately spends player control
delivery_techniques.how_it_works: Story beats play in the same engine and, where possible, while the player still controls the character; Half-Life-style scripted sequences trigger on location or action (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scripted_sequence). Celeste plays its ending as a final level instead of a film (https://cutscenes.substack.com/p/celestes-happy-ending-doesnt-exist). Hollow Knight's reviewer notes that losing control of the silent Knight is jarring precisely because player and avatar feel unified (GDC review PDF above). Godot supports this with AnimationPlayer method-call tracks (https://docs.godotengine.org/en/stable/classes/class_animation.html) and process_mode so a story UI can run while gameplay is paused (https://docs.godotengine.org/en/stable/tutorials/scripting/pausing_games.html).
delivery_techniques.cost_to_build: Medium-high; the largest single build. A StoryBeat resource (ordered steps), a sequencer in the presentation layer, an input/AI lock, skip and save-safety, and a way to stage actors that respects the ECS rule that only ViewSyncSystem touches nodes (e.g. a Cinematic mode and command queue a system consumes). Today main.gd only freezes the tick through room_ending (scripts/main.gd:132-133).
delivery_techniques.fit_for_us: Required for the wake in T1, the child noticing at B1, boss intro and defeat beats, and the ending. Principle: control is the story's currency. Keep early beats short and non-stealing so the King's direction lock (enemy-behavior-bible.md:361-364, 381-382) lands as a real violation.

delivery_techniques.technique: Fourth-wall child layer: the hand, the shadow, the crayon
delivery_techniques.how_it_works: The frame story is physical. The Plucky Squire lets its hero leave the storybook into the owner's real bedroom, with narration and words as puzzle pieces (https://www.unrealengine.com/en-US/developer-interviews/the-plucky-squire-blends-2d-and-3d-visuals-in-aesthetically-pleasing-and-mechanically-interesting-ways; https://www.cbr.com/plucky-squire-james-turner-interview/). OneShot casts the player as a god separate from the protagonist (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/OneShot). The Stanley Parable asks what happens if you disobey the narrator, and the narrator responds (https://www.gamespot.com/articles/breaking-out-of-the-routine-player-agency-in-the-stanley-parable/1100-6413312/). Undertale breaks the fourth wall and hints at other playthroughs (https://www.gamedeveloper.com/design/the-hidden-level-design-of-undertale).
delivery_techniques.example_game: The Plucky Squire, OneShot, The Stanley Parable, Undertale
delivery_techniques.cost_to_build: Medium. A hand/shadow actor and presenter, crayon draw FX, and data-driven ChildAction events (draw, move block, place paper) that tie into the GP.5 interventions (docs/design/gp5-child-intervention-system-spec.md). Presentation reads events only.
delivery_techniques.fit_for_us: Core of the premise, but the tone must stay gentle: the child is curious, sometimes scared, never sarcastic (nar3:25-29; gdd.md:447-449). Keep the child from explaining mechanics (nar1:81-87); show hesitation (the hand hovering) instead of lines.

delivery_techniques.how_it_works: Make the failure state part of the relationship. Hades advances the story on every death and victory (https://gdconf.com/news/dive-dialogue-hades-gdc-2021); Kasavin says dying becomes a return home rather than a catastrophe (https://www.inlander.com/archive/hades-writer-greg-kasavin-on-how-he-made-video-game-deaths-drive-a-feel-good/article_f508bf3c-7c29-5586-80ed-1cd615017dc1.html). Celeste respawns almost instantly, converting failure into education (https://theplayjournal.com/celeste-review/). Gris removes fail states entirely (https://www.redbull.com/us-en/gris-preview-interview).
delivery_techniques.cost_to_build: Low-medium. Death/attempt counters in story flags, a BarkTable keyed by zone, boss and attempt count, and a short reset animation (the hand sets the pawn back on its square).
delivery_techniques.fit_for_us: Very high: the game already says 'THE CHILD RESETS THE BOARD' (scripts/main.gd:296) and GP.6 wants low-punishment room resets (docs/design/gp6-failure-checkpoint-rules-spec.md:11-27). The child can grow worried, then encouraging, then quiet. Budget a few tiers per boss with once-only and cooldown rules, because Hades-scale variety is unaffordable.

delivery_techniques.technique: Bosses as story carriers (belief, phase, defeat beat)
delivery_techniques.how_it_works: A boss embodies a belief and the fight dramatizes challenging it. Cuphead's whole plot advances boss by boss, each a debtor to the Devil (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cuphead). Ueda doubted the idea of feeling good after beating monsters, so Shadow of the Colossus plays sad music after each kill (https://www.gamedeveloper.com/design/fumito-ueda-on-weaving-empathy-into-victory-in-i-shadow-of-the-colossus-i-). Undertale's Asgore destroys the Mercy button at the start of his fight (https://dl.acm.org/doi/full/10.1145/3815598.3815657). Phases need purpose, as with Ornstein and Smough where the second phase changes the fight (https://itch.io/blog/1024105/designing-the-perfect-boss-battle-a-game-developers-holy-grail.amp).
delivery_techniques.example_game: Cuphead, Shadow of the Colossus, Undertale, Dark Souls, Hollow Knight
delivery_techniques.cost_to_build: Depends on the unbuilt boss framework (audit EN lane: no boss has phases). Add a BossStory resource: what_it_believes, intro_beat, phase_beats[], defeat_beat, bark_table, rule_held (the Book page), and hub_flag set on defeat.
delivery_techniques.fit_for_us: High. nar1:93-99 gives roles and nar5:11-17 gives the budget: one intro, one personality behavior, one phase beat, one defeat beat, no speeches in combat. Add a quiet sorrow beat on defeat: pieces 'become ordinary toys again' (gdd.md:423) with a held silence, so beating them costs something, as Ueda intended.

delivery_techniques.how_it_works: Sound carries pace, suspense and release; Inside's talk argues for the game and audio engine talking both ways (https://www.gdcvault.com/play/1023731/A-Game-That-Listens-The). Journey's prototyping began with the music (https://www.gamedeveloper.com/audio/video-designing-a-new-emotional-experience-in-i-journey-i-), and silence marks key Ico beats (https://www.superjumpmagazine.com/how-minimalism-and-the-japanese-concept-of-ma-jian-defined-ico/).
delivery_techniques.example_game: Inside, Journey, Shadow of the Colossus, Ico
delivery_techniques.cost_to_build: Medium. A music/ambience state controller driven by story flags (leitmotifs, stems), and sound routed only through the main.gd bridge per CLAUDE.md. Composition is owner/asset work.
delivery_techniques.fit_for_us: High. T1 may be silent (t1 spec:286-301). The finale removes the child's voice and most ambience (gdd.md:510), which only works if the child's voice and room tone were established earlier. A music-box leitmotif for the child would pay off.

delivery_techniques.how_it_works: Deliberate pauses that do not advance plot give a sense of place and character and make emotional moments stand out; Ico's sofa save point is the model (https://www.superjumpmagazine.com/how-minimalism-and-the-japanese-concept-of-ma-jian-defined-ico/). Lazzaro notes players alternate between kinds of fun, so a calm key is part of a strong rhythm (https://www.nicolelazzaro.com/the4-keys-to-fun/).
delivery_techniques.cost_to_build: Low: a Rest/Sit interaction marker, a music change, no combat.
delivery_techniques.fit_for_us: High. The hub (H1) and the room before every boss become safe, tender rooms: sit with a fallen piece, look out the window at the night. This is where the player can feel the story instead of being told it.

delivery_techniques.technique: Companion bond through verbs, not lines
delivery_techniques.how_it_works: Ico's hand-holding is a held button; letting go leaves Yorda vulnerable, so responsibility is felt as a verb (https://puzzlebyrinth.com/en/articles/designer-ueda). Journey allows only a chirp and hides names until the credits (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Journey_(2012_video_game); https://gdconf.com/news/making-evocative-games-thatgamecompanys-jenova-chen-gdc-podcast-ep-10).
delivery_techniques.cost_to_build: Low-medium: two or three small pawn verbs (look up toward the child, stand with a fallen piece, call) wired to flags and barks.
delivery_techniques.fit_for_us: High. The Believe meter (gdd.md:229-235) makes asking for help cost something; make the act of asking emotional (the hand hesitates, then arrives) rather than a menu spell, and keep help changing the room, not HP (v2:674).

delivery_techniques.how_it_works: Short, self-contained episodes give each side character a tiny arc. Toem is a series of locations where a young protagonist does good deeds for curious characters (https://www.destructoid.com/reviews/toem-wholesome-photography-game-review/); its team describes the design path in the postmortem (https://www.gamedeveloper.com/production/postmortem-toem). A Short Hike keeps its story light but built around personal worries and a parent-relationship ending (https://gamepilgrim.com/2020/02/26/developer-interview-adam-robinson-yu/). The Hollow Knight review lists saving grubs and visiting Quirrell as choices made out of wanting to do good (GDC review PDF above).
delivery_techniques.example_game: Toem, A Short Hike, Hollow Knight
delivery_techniques.cost_to_build: Low code (an Interactable plus a tiny beat), moderate writing and art.
delivery_techniques.fit_for_us: The three optional rescues (gdd.md:547) become one-screen vignettes, each a white piece with a want (the Rook that always fell in line, the Bishop afraid of off-diagonals). They fill the hub (hub evolution gdd.md:303-310) and give the ending its 'small variations by rescues'.

delivery_techniques.technique: Hub evolution and world state as memory
delivery_techniques.how_it_works: The world visibly remembers what the player did. The GDD already lays out the hub changing after each boss (gdd.md:303-310); Unpacking carries leftover objects between moves so the player infers time passing (https://www.gamedeveloper.com/marketing/unpacking-a-narrative-through-1-000-household-items).
delivery_techniques.cost_to_build: Low: StateVariant nodes keyed to story flags, applied on zone load (Godot ConfigFile save already exists in WorldState).
delivery_techniques.fit_for_us: Very high payoff per unit of work. It is the player's visible proof of effort and the cheapest way to make the child's help feel earned.

delivery_techniques.technique: Endings that are played, bookended and designed first
delivery_techniques.how_it_works: Memory overweights the peak and the end (https://dl.acm.org/doi/fullHtml/10.1145/3582437.3587195; https://www.benlafreniere.ca/assets/papers/p5608-gutwin.pdf). Celeste's ending is a played final climb with callbacks to the opening (https://epiloguegaming.com/playing-the-narrative-celeste/). Journey returns to its opening dune and reveals companion names at the credits (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Journey_(2012_video_game)). Brothers' finale needs no tutorial because the player's habit is the payload (Kotaku link above). Hades closes its family conflict with a shared meal (Inlander link above).
delivery_techniques.cost_to_build: Medium. An Ending sequence resource (beats plus flag-driven variants), a credits scene over the live ending image, and a post-game title-screen state (e.g. the board with one square empty).
delivery_techniques.fit_for_us: Highest leverage. The approved image (morning, quiet board, pawn just outside the board by a blue line, the child leaves it there: nar1:105-118) is a bookend of the T1 silent board, and 'leaves it there' is the child's arc completing (gdd.md:441). Build the ending sequence and the King's box-closing before polishing the middle.

mechanics_as_story: Lift the rules one at a time (Gris/Celeste logic: new ability equals emotional change). As built, the pawn moves in four cardinal directions from the first frame, so the GDD's first backward step (gdd.md:316-324; v2:211-214) has no mechanical meaning. Option: a short prologue where the pawn can only march forward like a chess pawn, then T1's first backward step is the first rule break. The same DirectionLock component later powers the King's 'Lock Direction' and the finale where memories of each rescued piece restore one direction at a time (gdd.md:366-373; enemy-behavior-bible.md:361). The same verb opens and closes the game. Sources for the method: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gris and https://epiloguegaming.com/playing-the-narrative-celeste/.

The unassisted diagonal step as payload. Make diagonal movement the one thing the pawn never does (including for the player, who will try Shift+dir or two keys and be denied). The final strike is a diagonal taken by choice (gdd.md:373; enemy-behavior-bible.md:390). Brothers' ending works because the player's long-trained habit becomes the emotional mechanic with no tutorial (https://kotaku.com/brothers-tale-of-two-sons-remake-ending-older-younger-1851302128).

Each boss unlock negates that boss's belief, so learning a verb is the plot: Knight (pride in status and the leap) teaches the Rule Step; Bishop (faith in written lines) teaches the Chalk Path, redrawing the line; Rook (force, walls, straight lines) teaches the Eraser Guard, where standing still is brave (v2:438); the Queen takes help away; the King closes the box. Roles are from nar1:93-99; unlock list from v2:567-590.

Make the player obey before freeing them. Papers, Please conveys bureaucracy by making the player process rules under pressure (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludonarrative_dissonance; https://www.firstpersonscholar.com/the-art-of-papers-please/). A brief, fair sequence before the finale where the board's marked rules are physically displayed on cards or squares (enemy-behavior-bible.md Phase 2) and the player must comply to survive makes the later 'refusal' mean something. Keep it short; this is the one place the game is allowed to feel oppressive.

Calling for help is a relationship act. Asking costs a Believe segment (gdd.md:229-235). Let the hand hesitate before arriving (nar1:87), show its shadow crossing the board as a telegraph, and make the finale deny the call: the player presses the help input out of habit and nothing comes (the King 'closes the box', gdd.md:272, enemy-behavior-bible.md:364). The reflex being refused is the loss, in the same way Brothers uses a trained reflex (Kotaku link above). The last beat returns the hand without controlling the pawn (gdd.md:414).

Standing still as courage. Eraser Guard and waiting through a Rook's declared line are acts of bravery (v2:438). Wait-then-strike timing is also what the wake/T3 tutorial teaches ('Wait for the warning. Strike.': t3_first_pawn_clash.tscn:11). Reward patience with a bark or a held beat of music so players feel the choice was seen.

Standing with the fallen (mourning verb). A single confirm-press next to a fallen white piece or the dead King plays a silent beat: the pawn bows, the child's shadow stills, a music-box note sounds. It is optional, costs seconds and gives the opening a way to be sad that the player performs. The GDD's rescued-piece reflections (gdd.md:434) and the three optional rescues (gdd.md:547) build on the same verb; Hollow Knight's reviewer cites optional kindness as characterization (GDC review PDF: https://media.gdcvault.com/gdc2020/GameNarrativeReview/Gabriel%20St.%20Onge_Hollow%20Knight%20Narrative%20Review.pdf).

Defeat as 'becoming a toy again'. When a boss or captain falls (gdd.md:423), swap its piece for a plain toy and hold a beat of silence and a distinct soft sound; the pawn pauses. Ueda's sad music after each colossus kill is the model for making victory cost something (https://www.gamedeveloper.com/design/fumito-ueda-on-weaving-empathy-into-victory-in-i-shadow-of-the-colossus-i-). This answers nar1:139 ('black side not purely evil') without making the enemies sympathetic in combat.

Beat the boss with the boss's own rule (Rook destroys its throne: gdd.md:407; Bishop cannot see the crayon line: gdd.md:400). Design each fight so the winning move uses what the boss refuses to change; the player discovers the thesis by solving it, not by reading a line. Undertale's Asgore taking away Mercy is the same pattern of a boss altering the verbs (https://dl.acm.org/doi/full/10.1145/3815598.3815657).

Death as the child resetting the board. Show the hand placing the pawn back on its start square after each loss (scripts/main.gd:296 already names it). Gentle change across attempts: the first reset is silent, repeated resets draw a worried or encouraging child bark, and the old GDD whisper 'Try another way' (gdd.md:323) fits best as an offer after several deaths, not a prologue line. Method: Hades, https://gdconf.com/news/dive-dialogue-hades-gdc-2021.

Camera scale as feeling. The pawn is tiny, the hand is large and smooth (gdd.md:462). Use the same zoomed-out bedroom framing for the opening shot, the Queen's address to the child and the final morning shot, so the first and last images rhyme (Journey returns to its opening dune: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Journey_(2012_video_game)). Light and contrast direct attention and mood (Carson: https://www.gamedeveloper.com/design/environmental-storytelling-creating-immersive-3d-worlds-using-lessons-learned-from-the-theme-park-industry).

Optional authorship (proposal, owner decision): in the last room the pawn 'chooses a new rule' (v2:65, 529). Let the player pick one line from a short list of owner-written rules to appear on a blank page of the Book, changing only the closing text, never the ending. It gives the freedom theme a verb without breaking the no-branching scope rule (gdd.md:555) and is an easy place for the owner to substitute their own wording.

structure_options.shape: Act I: Prologue + T1-H1 (loss, sword, first fight, the child notices at B1). Act IIa: Knight and Bishop (agency to trust), ending on the midpoint reveal that the war began as the child's lonely game (gdd.md:355). Act IIb: Rook and Queen (pressure; the Queen addresses the child and help is disrupted: gdd.md:360-361, v2:458-459). Low point: the Black King closes the box (gdd.md:366-373). Act III: unassisted climax, then morning. This is nar1's ladder (nar1:21-48) in three acts.
structure_options.pros: Matches the approved docs one to one. Dunniway recommends front-loading training in the first two acts so the last act starts when players know how to play, and a clear low point before the climax (https://www.gamedeveloper.com/design/using-the-hero-s-journey-in-games; https://www.linkedin.com/pulse/using-heros-journey-game-level-design-storytelling-troy-dunniway). Familiar to testers.
structure_options.cons: Three-act fits games only partly because games have play that advances neither character nor plot (https://gamedesignskills.com/game-design/three-act-structure/), and the midpoint is the weakest joint (http://gamedesignaspect.blogspot.com/2014/08/writers-stop-obsessing-over-three-act.html). A five-boss middle reads as a checklist unless each boss changes the child-pawn relationship.

structure_options.shape: Ki: the silent rug aftermath (Act 0-1). Sho: four districts deepen pawn and child without changing the premise. Ten (about 60-70%): the reframing twist that the war is a child's game that may be put away, delivered by the Queen's speech to the child (gdd.md:355-361). Ketsu: morning, pawn outside the board.
structure_options.pros: Needs no hateful villain, which suits nar1:139 and the gentle tone. The twist reframes rather than escalates, so it can be the emotional peak. The structure is used by Nintendo's level designers as introduce, develop, twist, conclude (https://mcvuk.com/business-news/publishing/video-nintendos-level-design-secrets-in-four-steps/; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kish%C5%8Dtenketsu). The room formula already in v2:627-638 is this shape.
structure_options.cons: The Black King fight is a confrontation, so the whole game cannot be 'without conflict'; Wikipedia notes that label is a simplification (Kishotenketsu link above). Players expecting escalation may find the sho section slow. Few collaborators have used it.

structure_options.shape: Ordinary world (rug), call (the child notices), ally (the child), threshold (H1), ordeals (bosses), abyss (the box closes), return (morning).
structure_options.pros: Gives a vocabulary of emotional stations; Journey followed the monomyth (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Journey_(2012_video_game)). Dunniway uses it to pace training and level flow (Game Developer link above).
structure_options.cons: Pulls toward 'chosen one', which contradicts a pawn 'not chosen by rank' (nar1:58) and 'no heroic chosen-one staging' (docs/production/t1-white-kings-fall-production-spec.md:56). 'Return with the elixir' only works if the elixir is freedom, not a crown. Heavy for 1-2 hours.

structure_options.structure: String of pearls (chained mini-arcs per district)
structure_options.shape: Each district is a complete 15-20 minute micro-story with its own lesson (nar4:13-19: status is not strength; written rules can be redrawn; walls can be resisted; control is fragile; confront the system), linked by two threads: child trust and the Book of House Rules.
structure_options.pros: Matches production reality: the owner draws and writes district by district, and a partial build still lands. Supports the flexible Bishop/Rook order (gdd.md:294-299). Chaining several cycles is a recognised approach for episodic structures (https://ursb.me/en/posts/weekly-8/); Cuphead and Toem work episodically (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cuphead; https://www.destructoid.com/reviews/toem-wholesome-photography-game-review/).
structure_options.cons: Episodic feel and the risk the docs warn about: story repeats the same beat (nar4:25-29). Needs deliberate through-lines and a rising emotional line across districts.

structure_options.structure: One-night frame (proposal): dusk to morning as the spine
structure_options.shape: The opening is lamp-lit or moonlit; each defeated boss advances the light in the window and the room tint; the ending is morning light (nar1:107) and the child 'asleep or smiling' (v2:557). Keyed to the count of bosses beaten, not their order.
structure_options.pros: Nearly free (global tint, hub window prop, music), gives a clock the player feels without text, and unifies a chained structure; the ending is built in. Light and contrast as storytelling are standard environmental technique (Carson link above); Gris uses colour restoration as its arc (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gris).
structure_options.cons:
Needs the owner to confirm the 'one night' premise and that the child falls asleep or stays awake at the end; district order flexibility must not break the lighting logic. This is my suggestion; no doc states it.

RECOMMENDED HYBRID: macro three-act (for pacing, midpoint and a true low point), micro kishotenketsu per district (teach, develop, twist, test; the room formula in v2:627-638), the one-night frame as the thread, and a quiet-key rule from Lazzaro (https://www.nicolelazzaro.com/the4-keys-to-fun/) so every boss is preceded by a calm room.

systems_needed: 1. Narrative text as data, keyed and translatable. Every player-facing string (room messages, prompts, dialogue, barks, Book pages, titles, credits) lives in a keyed table (Godot tr() / CSV translations, per https://docs.godotengine.org/en/stable/tutorials/i18n/internationalizing_games.html), never in .gd or hardcoded in .tscn. Migrate today's strings (main.gd:147-150, 280-296, 416-425; the six room messages; PlayerUnlockMarker.message) and add a headless lint that fails on a hardcoded story string or a missing key. English plus one more locale from day one so layouts survive longer strings.

2. A font and text-size policy that survives the canvas: a story font readable at 640x360 (about 10 px minimum with extra line height; Xbox guidance of 28 px at 1080p is about 9 px at 360p: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/gaming/accessibility/xbox-accessibility-guidelines/104), verified against Vietnamese diacritics (itch.io CC0 fonts list some with Vietnamese coverage, none confirmed at pixel size: https://itch.io/c/5127941/cc0-fonts), a text-size option and a high-contrast box (IGDA Top Ten: https://igda-gasig.org/how/game-accessibility-top-ten-se/).

3. Speaker resource: id, name key, color, blip stream, pitch range, portrait or icon set, text style. The child gets a soft blue-tinged voice; pieces get distinct blips; the pawn is silent (emote icons only).

4. DialogueSequence resource and presenter: ordered lines (speaker, text key, expression, pause, sfx or flag hooks, once-only, conditions), RichTextLabel typewriter via visible_ratio (https://docs.godotengine.org/en/stable/classes/class_richtextlabel.html), BBCode emotion effects (https://docs.godotengine.org/en/stable/tutorials/ui/bbcode_in_richtextlabel.html), advance and fast-forward, text speed option, a bubble or banner placement that never covers danger cells (gdd.md:522), and a world-space and a screen-space style. Max four lines per sequence by default (gdd.md:431).

5. Minimal choice support, not branching: a single 'pick one' prompt that writes a flag (for the optional rule-authorship beat or rest-spot choices). No dialogue trees: branching campaigns are out of scope (gdd.md:555). A dialogue addon is optional; if the owner wants one, Dialogue Manager 4 (MIT, GDScript, Godot 4.6+, stateless so flags stay in WorldState) is the best fit (https://github.com/nathanhoad/godot_dialogue_manager; comparison https://storyflow-editor.com/blog/best-godot-dialogue-systems/). Dialogic 2 is alpha and keeps its own state (same comparison), and Yarn Spinner C# and godot-ink need a .NET build (https://docs.yarnspinner.dev/yarn-spinner-for-godot/godot-gdscript; https://github.com/paulloz/godot-ink). CLAUDE.md requires built-ins first and the owner's yes before any dependency.

6. Story flags and counters in WorldState: story_flags (bool by id), counters (death_count by zone/boss, rescued_pieces, bosses_beaten, child_trust), saved with a version bump next to unlocked_rule_ids and player_unlock_ids (scripts/world/world_state.gd:10-22). A condition grammar in data: has_flag, not_flag, counter >= n, bosses_beaten >= n, zone is X.

7. StoryTrigger markers (editor-placed like PlayerUnlockMarker and GridMarker): trigger kinds are enter zone, step on cell, room cleared, enemy defeated, boss phase changed, pickup taken, idle at a cell for N seconds (lingering at the fallen king), Nth death, flag becomes true. They emit a story_beat event on the existing drain_events queue; main.gd's bridge hands it to the narrative director. Systems never play dialogue (CLAUDE.md: presentation consumes drain_events only).

8. StoryBeat resource and sequencer (the cutscene system): ordered steps (wait, dialogue, camera move or zoom, play actor clip, show or hide prop, hand enters or exits, crayon draw, music state, sfx, set flag, fade, title card, lock or unlock input). Implemented with AnimationPlayer method tracks, Tween and process_mode (https://docs.godotengine.org/en/stable/classes/class_animation.html; https://docs.godotengine.org/en/stable/tutorials/scripting/pausing_games.html). Must be skippable, safe to skip (same end state as playing), save-safe, and honor the ECS rule: a Cinematic mode plus a command queue a system consumes, so only ViewSyncSystem touches nodes. Each beat carries purpose and emotion_tag fields for the owner and for lint.

9. Bark system: BarkTable resources (trigger event, speaker, lines, weight, priority, cooldown, once-only, conditions), a selector in the bridge, one bark at a time, suppression during danger telegraphs unless tiny, and counters so lines do not repeat (Far Cry 2 / Hades approach: https://kotaku.com/why-video-game-characters-say-such-ridiculous-things-5921878; https://gdconf.com/news/dive-dialogue-hades-gdc-2021). Barks for the child, white survivors, black pieces, and pawn emotes.

10. Death and retry narrative hooks: a hand-resets-the-board animation and per-attempt BarkTable tiers for each zone and boss (first death silent, later worry or encouragement, optional 'try another way' offer after several), driven by death_count flags. Keeps GP.6's low-punishment reset (gp6:11-27) emotional instead of mechanical.

11. Child layer toolkit: hand and shadow actor, crayon-draw FX, paper/block/path placement visuals as ChildAction events (shared with the GP.5 interventions), reaction states (watching, worried, delighted, hesitant), a presence level tied to child_trust, a voice style distinct from kingdom voices (gdd.md:508), and a mute mode for the finale (gdd.md:510).

12. Interactable markers: confirm-press near a prop, fallen piece or rescued survivor plays a one-line beat or an emote bubble; supports environmental lore, 'stand with the fallen' and rescue vignettes. Highlight state shown through the existing yellow-for-interactable language (gdd.md:483).

13. Book of House Rules v2: page states (unread, read, new, rewritten), the child's margin notes, crossed-out and re-inked amendments, pages for the Black Captain, bosses and weapons, unlock on 'seen in combat', and the world frozen while open (audit UI.3 gaps). Extra pages for keepsakes (the child's drawings, rescued pieces) as optional lore, never required homework (ui3:21-30).

14. Boss story hooks: BossStory resource (what_it_believes, intro_beat, phase_beats[], defeat_beat, bark_table, rule_held, defeat prop swap, hub flag), fired from the boss framework's phase and defeat events; Black Line seal beat; the 'becomes a toy again' swap and silence. Enforces nar5:11-17: one intro, one personality behavior, one phase beat, one defeat beat, no speeches mid-combat.

15. StateVariant nodes for hub and room evolution: show, hide or swap by flag condition, applied at zone load (hub evolution gdd.md:303-310; rescued pieces; rug tidied; the night-to-morning tint if the one-night frame is adopted). Pure data, no per-room scripts.

16. Audio director: music and ambience states keyed to story flags (silent T1, hub theme, child leitmotif, boss themes, finale subtraction), played only from the bridge. Includes a stinger channel for key beats and a duck for dialogue (default_bus_layout.tres already has SFX/Music/UI buses).
17. Cinematic camera moves in CameraRig: focus on target, pan, hold, zoom out to the bedroom scale for the opening, the Queen's address and the ending (rhyming first and last frames).

18. Frame screens: title screen (with Continue from the WorldState autosave and New Game that clears it), chapter or time-of-night cards, pause menu with Resume, Restart room, Book, Settings and Quit, credits and epilogue, and a post-game state (e.g. the title board with one square empty). Also settings: text size and speed, reduced shake (audit UI.6), subtitles for child sounds.

19. Ending system: an Ending resource (beats plus flag-driven variants for rescues, gdd.md:547), a credits scroll over the live final image, and a decision point for which of the three ending versions ships (gdd.md:375-380 vs v2:549 vs nar1:105-118).

20. Placeholder-complete script: write a full v0 script for every beat, bark and Book page with placeholder text clearly marked, each tagged with purpose and emotion so the base plays start to finish and the owner can rewrite words and art without breaking structure.

21. Owner authoring and debug tools: a story test room that fires any beat or bark on demand, a flags and counters debug panel, a script exporter that dumps all text in play order for proofreading, hot-reload of translation tables, and validators (beat never reachable, speaker missing, flag read but never set, flag set but never read, every boss has intro, phase and defeat beats, every key present in every locale).

22. Narrative tests in the headless suite (tests/run_tests.gd): beat graph reachability, skip-equals-play end state, no soft-lock when a beat is interrupted by death, save and load round trip of flags, localization completeness, and a check that no sequence exceeds the line budget.

23. Emotion-curve metadata: an emotion_tag (calm, tension, release, awe, loss) and an optional intensity on every beat and room, with a lint that flags long stretches without a calm key and requires the designated peaks (the Queen reveal, the box closing, the final step, the ending) to be marked. Rationale: players alternate between kinds of fun (https://www.nicolelazzaro.com/the4-keys-to-fun/) and memory weights the peak and end (https://dl.acm.org/doi/fullHtml/10.1145/3582437.3587195).

24. Accessibility for narrative: skip and replay of every beat, never timed-only text, pause during dialogue except tiny barks, subtitles and captions for meaningful audio, at most two lines and about 40 characters per line (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/gaming/accessibility/xbox-accessibility-guidelines/104), and reduced-flash and reduced-shake settings that apply to story beats too.
